cells.quote: Based on the arithmetic mean, more (43%) of the students meaningfully engaged in the off-ramp transition during the ‘bridge’ space following the 1st year lecture in the type 2 timetable, whereas less (19%) of the students meaningfully engaged in the off-ramp transition in the type 1 timetable (see Fig.1). cells.note: Qualitative interview and observation evidence; no numerical effect size was reported.

D.comparison: teacher-centred transmission in the lecture theatre

cells.quote: The affordances and flexibility of the breakout space meant that students under their own control could form pairs and small learning groups more easily than in the row-by-row lecture theatre. cells.note: The study observed postponed, hidden and student-directed pedagogic interactions rather than measuring learning performance.

O.outcome_detail: accounting for contextual variation and FATE-related issues

cells.quote: This approach has difficulties accounting for contextual variation (e.g., classroom instructional contexts or sociocultural identities of learners) and often treats them as noise (Holstein et al., 2017). Special attention to variation is needed to attend to FATE in classroom contextual and organizational structures that impact teaching and learning (Gomez et al., 2020).
cells.note: The study presents a theoretical argument, not an empirical comparison.

O.outcome_detail: recognizing and addressing FATE issues during practice and use

cells.quote: However, this set of approaches tends to engage users primarily in early stages of the design process with the goal of using feedback to redesign the technology, which can limit our ability to recognize and address FATE-related issues that arise in practice and through use. Continuous improvement expands upon these approaches through systematic inquiry and including stakeholders in all stages.
cells.note: The study argues that Continuous Improvement extends participatory and co-design approaches; it does not report an empirical effect.

O.outcome_detail: learning from variation and making systems work across contexts

cells.quote: However, the work is often siloed within a single setting over a long time frame (see Wang & Hannafin, 2005) and it remains difficult to replicate local practices from one setting to another (Design-Based Research Collective, 2003). Thus, DBR benefits research that is interested in similar settings (Amiel & Reeves, 2008). We will point out shortly that IS can support learning from variation across contexts because the testing and iteration are more extensive and include new social arrangements (i.e., Networked Improvement Communities).
cells.note: The study presents this as a methodological argument rather than a tested treatment comparison.
